name: Galaico-Portuguese

stress.notes: Galaico-Portuguese stress: paroxytone default, oxytone on the consonant/high-vowel endings shared with modern Portuguese, and a written accent overrides both. Medieval scribal practice was inconsistent about marking accents, but the axis is the same as its descendants and any accent present in the input must attract stress rather than be dropped. DIPHTHONGS are declared so the bundled syllabifier counts nuclei correctly; without them a vowel run collapses to one nucleus and the stress (and its conditioned reduction) lands on the wrong vowel (Cunha & Cintra, Nova Gramática do Português Contemporâneo, §Ditongos). ⟨uí⟩ is deliberately absent: an acute on a stressed ⟨i⟩ or ⟨u⟩ after another vowel is the orthography's own hiatus mark, written precisely "quando antecedidas de uma vogal com que não formam ditongo" (Acordo Ortográfico da Língua Portuguesa 1990, Base X §1 — juízes, ruína, influíste, saída). A spelling that writes ⟨uí⟩ is stating that the two vowels are separate nuclei, so listing it here made the bundled syllabifier read ru-í-do as ruí-do.

ancestors.notes: Primary descent from Hispanic Vulgar Latin. The NW Iberian development of spoken Latin.
Gallaecian Celtic substrate: strongest in NW Iberia. Castro culture, toponyms, possible influence on nasal vowel development.
Lusitanian substrate: pre-Celtic IE language of western Iberia. Possible influence on /v/≠/b/ preservation.
Suebi (Germanic) superstrate in Gallaecia (411–585 CE): Kingdom of the Suebi. ~200 place names, vocabulary (guerra, roubar, branco).
Visigothic superstrate shared with all Ibero-Romance.
Occitan adstrate: nh and lh digraphs inherited from occitan
Mozarabic adstrate: less intense in the NW than in central/southern Iberia due to shorter Moorish presence.
Andalusi Arabic adstrate: less intense in the NW than in central/southern Iberia due to shorter Moorish presence.

Asturleonese/Leonese adstrate: the Kingdom of Asturias and León was the dominant political power of Christian Iberia during the formative period of Galaico-Portuguese (8th–12th c.). The Leonese chancery language influenced administrative writing conventions, shared the 4-way sibilant system, and contributed some lexical and phonological features across the border. The split between the Galaico-Portuguese and Asturleonese traditions became clear only after the County of Portugal's independence (~1139).

notes: Galaico-Portuguese (~9th–14th c. CE). The shared ancestor of modern Galician and Portuguese. Attested in troubadour lyric poetry (Cantigas de Santa Maria, cantigas de amigo, cantigas de amor — >1,600 texts), early legal documents (Notícia de Torto ~1214, Testamento de D. Afonso II ~1214). KEY FEATURES: (1) Medieval 4-way sibilant contrast: /ts/ ⟨ç⟩ vs /d͡z/ ⟨z⟩ vs /s/ ⟨ss⟩ vs /z/ ⟨-s-⟩. (2) /ʎ/ ⟨lh⟩, /ɲ/ ⟨nh⟩ digraph convention from Occitan. (3) /b/ ≠ /v/ preserved. (4) F- preserved (filho, not hijo). (5) /ou/ still a true diphthong. (6) Nasal vowels developing but not fully phonemicised. The split into Galician and Portuguese is conventionally dated to ~mid-14th c. when the Portuguese court settled in Lisbon and Galician fell under Castilian influence. Source: Maia (1986), Castro (2006), Teyssier (1982).

sources.notes: The orthographic standard itself. Base VIII lists the ditongos abertos ⟨-éi éu ói⟩; Base IX explains why paroxytone ⟨ei oi⟩ go unaccented; Base X §1 accents ⟨i u⟩ after a vowel precisely when the two do NOT form a diphthong, which is what makes ⟨uí⟩ a written hiatus.

location.notes: Glottolog's computed centroid for the Galician Romance family — a summary of a whole clade's range, not a place anyone speaks.
